results.title_inferred: Artemisia (Mugwort) — Macer Floridus on its virtues
results.original_text: Artemisia — Mugwort. Macer Floridus: Among herbs artemisia is queen. It warms, expels worms, provokes menstruation, aids the traveller against fatigue. The root taken in wine drives out the stone. Applied to the navel it eases childbirth.
results.translation: Artemisia — Mugwort. Macer Floridus states: Among herbs, artemisia is queen. It has a warming property, expels intestinal worms, provokes menstruation, and aids the traveller in resisting fatigue. When the root is taken in wine, it expels the (bladder or kidney) stone. When applied to the navel, it eases childbirth.

entities_mentioned.name: Artemisia
entities_mentioned.notes: Classical and medieval sources consistently identify 'artemisia' with mugwort; the epithet 'queen of herbs' is a standard trope from Macer Floridus's De viribus herbarum.

results.translator_notes: Source text appears to be a modern English paraphrase/summary of the original Latin verses of Macer Floridus rather than a direct transcription of the Latin itself; no Latin original was provided for word-for-word rendering. The four indications (warming, vermifuge, emmenagogue, anti-fatigue for travelers) plus the two applications (root in wine for the stone; navel application for childbirth) are standard attributes assigned to artemisia in the Macer Floridus tradition.

results.title_inferred: Beta (Beet) — Medicinal Uses
results.original_text: Beta — Beet. The juice of black beet dropped into the nostrils purges the head. Taken in wine it helps against serpent bite. The leaves applied warm ease headache.
results.translation: Beet (Beta). The juice of black beet, dropped into the nostrils, purges [clears] the head. Taken in wine, it helps against snakebite. The leaves, applied warm, relieve headache.

entities_mentioned.name: Beta (black beet)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Beta vulgaris (beet, likely a dark-rooted or dark-leaved variety)
entities_mentioned.notes: Common in medieval herbals (following Macer Floridus' De viribus herbarum) as a purgative and vulnerary plant; 'black beet' likely denotes a variety with dark red or purplish roots/leaves, distinguished from white beet (Beta alba) in some herbal traditions.

results.translator_notes: The source text supplied is already in English rather than Latin or Czech; no OCR correction or translation from a foreign-language original was required. The entry follows the typical Macer Floridus format: plant name, preparation, and sequential list of indications (head-purging via nasal application, antidote for venom, topical relief for headache).

results.title_inferred: Vervain (Verbena) and Its Medicinal Uses
results.original_text: Verbena — Vervain. Vervain purges old fevers. Worn about the neck it heals scrofula and throat ailments. Taken with vinegar it helps the spleen and old sores.
results.translation: Vervain [Verbena]. Vervain purges chronic [long-standing] fevers. When worn about the neck, it heals scrofula [glandular swellings] and ailments of the throat. Taken with vinegar, it aids the spleen and heals old [chronic] sores.

entities_mentioned.name: Verbena
entities_mentioned.notes: A well-known medicinal herb in the Macer Floridus tradition, associated with amuletic and internal uses in medieval herbals.

results.translator_notes: The phrase 'old fevers' likely renders Latin 'febres veteres,' meaning chronic or recurring fevers rather than fevers of long duration in a single episode. 'Scrofula' (Latin 'scrofulae') refers to tubercular swellings of the lymph nodes, a common medieval diagnostic category. The amuletic use ('worn about the neck') reflects the sympathetic/apotropaic medicine typical of the Macer Floridus tradition.

results.title_inferred: Sage (Salvia) — Its Warming and Restorative Virtues
results.original_text: Salvia — Sage. Sage warms the sinews and drives out paralysis. The juice with wine drunk for forty days restores sensation to paralysed limbs. It sharpens memory and is good for the liver.
results.translation: Sage — Sage. Sage warms the sinews and drives out paralysis. Its juice, drunk with wine for forty days, restores sensation to paralysed limbs. It sharpens the memory and is beneficial for the liver.

entities_mentioned.name: Salvia
entities_mentioned.notes: Standard identification consistent with Macer Floridus tradition; sage was widely used in medieval pharmacology for nervous and hepatic complaints.

results.translator_notes: This entry follows the typical Macer Floridus formula: named plant, brief virtues, a specific preparation (juice in wine over a fixed duration), and indications (paralysis, memory, liver). The '40 days' regimen is a common numerological/therapeutic convention in medieval herbal texts, often symbolic as well as practical.

results.title_inferred: Rue (Ruta) — Properties and Uses
results.original_text: Ruta — Rue. Rue sharpens the sight and counteracts all poisons and venoms. Mixed with honey it draws poison from the bitten. It suppresses lust when eaten frequently.
results.translation: Rue — Rue. Rue sharpens the eyesight and counteracts all poisons and venoms. When mixed with honey, it draws out poison from those who have been bitten [by venomous animals]. When eaten frequently, it suppresses lust.

entities_mentioned.name: Ruta
entities_mentioned.notes: Standard identification in Macer Floridus tradition; rue was widely used in medieval pharmacy as an antidote and anaphrodisiac.

results.translator_notes: This entry follows the typical Macer Floridus structure closely: sight-sharpening, antidotal, and anti-libidinal properties are conventional attributions to rue in this herbal tradition. 'Bitten' likely refers to venomous animal bites (e.g., snakes, scorpions) per standard Macer usage, though the source text does not specify the biting agent.

entities_mentioned.name: Absinthium

results.title_inferred: Mentha (Mint) — Medicinal Uses
results.original_text: Mentha — Mint. Mint stops vomiting and hiccough. Applied with salt it cures dog bite. Taken with honey and vinegar it dissolves congealed blood. It restrains the flow of blood.
results.translation: Mint (Mentha). Mint stops vomiting and hiccups. When applied together with salt, it heals dog bites. Taken with honey and vinegar, it dissolves clotted blood. It also checks the flow of blood.

results.title_inferred: Nettle (Urtica) — Medicinal Uses
results.original_text: Urtica — Nettle. Nettle seed with wine and pepper provokes coition. The root with vinegar cures the mange. The boiled herb with alum stops bleeding. Taken in drink it clears mucus from the lungs.
results.translation: Nettle. Nettle seed taken with wine and pepper provokes sexual desire (coition). The root, applied with vinegar, cures scabies (the mange). The herb, boiled together with alum, stops bleeding. Taken as a drink, it clears phlegm/mucus from the lungs.

entities_mentioned.name: Urtica
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Urtica dioica (common nettle) or related Urtica species
entities_mentioned.notes: Standard identification for 'Urtica' in Macer Floridus and related medieval herbals; seeds, roots, and boiled herb are each used for distinct remedies.

results.title_inferred: Agrimony (Agrimonia) — Liver Purge, Wound Healing, and Tertian Fever Remedy
results.original_text: Agrimonia — Agrimony. Agrimonia cum aqua hepar purgat. Herba in vino cocta vulneribus prodest et morsum serpentis sanat. Bona est contra tertianam febrem in vino sumpta ante accessum.
results.translation: Agrimony. Agrimony taken with water purges the liver. The herb boiled in wine is beneficial for wounds and heals serpent bites. It is good against tertian fever when taken in wine before the onset of the fit.

entities_mentioned.name: Agrimonia
entities_mentioned.notes: Widely used in medieval herbals (following Macer Floridus' 'De viribus herbarum') for liver ailments, wound healing, and intermittent fevers such as tertian fever.

results.title_inferred: Macer Floridus, ch. 14: Lactuca (Lettuce)
results.original_text: Lactuca — Lettuce. Lettuce promotes sleep and restrains carnal desire. The juice taken with vinegar helps those suffering from inflammation of the liver. It increases milk in nursing women.
results.translation: Lettuce. Lettuce induces sleep and suppresses carnal desire. Its juice, taken with vinegar, helps those suffering from inflammation of the liver. It increases milk in nursing women.

results.title_inferred: Purslane (Portulaca) for Headache, Bile, and Internal Heat
results.original_text: Portulaca — Purslane. Purslane applied to the forehead cures headache from heat. The juice taken with vinegar and honey removes bile. It cools internal heat and quenches thirst.
results.translation: Purslane. Purslane, applied to the forehead, cures headache caused by heat [febrile or 'hot' headache]. Its juice, taken with vinegar and honey, removes [excess] bile. It cools internal heat and quenches thirst.

entities_mentioned.name: Portulaca
entities_mentioned.notes: Standard identification of Portulaca in Macer Floridus and related medieval herbals; consistently rendered as purslane in both Latin and vernacular traditions.

'Headache from heat' reflects the humoral theory concept of cephalalgia caused by excess heat (calor), and 'removes bile' reflects purgation of choleric (yellow bile) humor, consistent with purslane's traditional cooling (frigid/humid) qualities in Galenic pharmacology.

results.title_inferred: Albík's Regimen for the Emperor's Daily Health
results.original_text: Albík on imperial health regimen: The emperor should rise at the fourth hour, take light food in the morning, avoid strong wine before midday. Exercise should be moderate — neither excessive nor absent. Rest after the midday meal is beneficial but sleep should not exceed two hours in daylight.
results.translation: Albík on the regimen for the emperor's health: The emperor should rise at the fourth hour [approximately 10 a.m. by medieval reckoning, or four hours after sunrise], take a light meal in the morning, and avoid strong wine before midday. Physical exercise should be moderate—neither excessive nor entirely absent. Resting after the midday meal is beneficial, but daytime sleep should not exceed two hours.

entities_mentioned.name: strong wine (vinum forte)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Wine, likely a fortified or undiluted variety
entities_mentioned.notes: Referenced as a substance to be avoided before midday, consistent with medieval humoral dietetics warning against consuming strong drink on an empty stomach or too early in the day.

results.translator_notes: This passage belongs to the genre of the 'regimen sanitatis,' health advice literature attributed to the court physician Albík of Uničov (fl. early 15th century), written for Emperor Sigismund of Luxembourg. The 'fourth hour' likely follows the medieval convention of counting hours from sunrise, placing rising time in mid-morning by modern reckoning. No specific herbal or pharmacological entities are named in this excerpt; the content is regimen advice rather than a materia medica entry.

results.title_inferred: Albík's Advice on Digestion for Emperor Sigismund
results.original_text: Albík on digestion: After eating the emperor should walk one hundred paces or sit quietly. No cold water should be drunk immediately after meals. Lettuce and fennel aid digestion; onion and garlic in small amounts are beneficial to one of phlegmatic complexion.
results.translation: Albík on digestion: After eating, the emperor should walk one hundred paces or sit quietly. No cold water should be drunk immediately after meals. Lettuce and fennel aid digestion; onion and garlic, taken in small amounts, are beneficial to a person of phlegmatic complexion.

entities_mentioned.name: Lettuce
entities_mentioned.notes: Commonly recommended in medieval dietetics as a cooling, digestion-aiding food, often taken after meals.

entities_mentioned.name: Fennel
entities_mentioned.notes: Widely used in medieval medicine as a carminative to aid digestion and relieve flatulence.

entities_mentioned.name: Onion
entities_mentioned.notes: Considered warming in humoral theory; recommended in moderation for phlegmatic (cold and moist) constitutions.

entities_mentioned.name: Garlic
entities_mentioned.notes: Also considered hot and dry in humoral terms, counterbalancing phlegmatic coldness when used sparingly.

results.translator_notes: This passage reflects Galenic humoral dietetics, in which foods are chosen to balance the patient's complexion (here, phlegmatic = cold and moist). The advice to walk after meals and avoid cold water reflects standard medieval postprandial regimen (regimen sanitatis) guidance attributed to Albík of Uničov, physician to Emperor Sigismund.

results.title_inferred: Albík's Advice on Treating Fevers
results.original_text: Albík on fever: In tertian fever the patient should fast on the day of the paroxysm. Wormwood with wine taken before the onset of the attack gives relief. Agrimony with spring water is effective against quotidian fever. The patient should keep warm and avoid cold air.
results.translation: Albík on fever: In tertian fever, the patient should fast on the day of the paroxysm [the recurring feverish episode]. Wormwood taken with wine before the onset of the attack brings relief. Agrimony taken with spring water is effective against quotidian fever [a fever recurring daily]. The patient should keep warm and avoid cold air.

entities_mentioned.name: Wormwood
entities_mentioned.notes: Commonly used in medieval medicine for fevers and digestive ailments; bitter herb associated with feverfew-like remedies.

entities_mentioned.name: Agrimony
entities_mentioned.notes: Widely used in medieval herbals for fevers, liver ailments, and as a general tonic.

entities_mentioned.name: Tertian fever
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Likely a form of malaria (Plasmodium vivax or P. ovale infection) causing fever every third day
entities_mentioned.notes: Medieval fever classification based on periodicity; tertian = recurring every other day (i.e., on the 1st and 3rd day).

entities_mentioned.name: Quotidian fever
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Possibly daily-recurring malarial fever (Plasmodium falciparum) or another cyclic fever
entities_mentioned.notes: Medieval term for fever recurring every day, distinguished from tertian and quartan types.

results.translator_notes: The text reflects the medieval humoral system of fever classification (tertian, quartan, quotidian) based on periodicity of paroxysms, tied to supposed imbalance of bodily humors. Wormwood and agrimony were staple antipyretic and digestive herbs in medieval pharmacopoeia. No obvious OCR corruption or illegible sections in this passage.

results.title_inferred: Albík's Advice on Treating Battle Wounds
results.original_text: Albík on wounds in campaign: For wounds sustained in battle, apply plantain leaf bruised with salt immediately to stop bleeding. For deep wounds, pour wine into the cavity before closing. Honey mixed with white of egg draws out corruption. Wounds should be kept dry after the third day.
results.translation: Albík on wounds sustained during campaign: For wounds received in battle, apply bruised plantain leaf [plantago] mixed with salt immediately to staunch the bleeding. For deep wounds, pour wine into the wound cavity before closing it. Honey mixed with egg white [albumen ovi] draws out corrupt matter [putrefaction/pus]. After the third day, wounds should be kept dry.

entities_mentioned.name: plantain (plantago)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Plantago major (greater plantain) or Plantago lanceolata (ribwort plantain)
entities_mentioned.notes: Commonly used in medieval wound care for its astringent and hemostatic properties; bruising releases juices applied topically.

entities_mentioned.name: salt
entities_mentioned.notes: Used as an antiseptic and to promote wound contraction in traditional remedies.

entities_mentioned.name: wine
entities_mentioned.notes: Used as a cleansing agent for deep wounds; alcohol content provided rudimentary antisepsis.

entities_mentioned.name: honey
entities_mentioned.notes: Widely used in medieval and ancient medicine for wound healing due to antibacterial and osmotic properties.

entities_mentioned.name: egg white (albumen)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: egg albumen from Gallus gallus domesticus
entities_mentioned.notes: Applied topically, sometimes combined with honey, believed to draw out corrupt or putrid matter from wounds.

results.translator_notes: The supplied source text was already rendered in modern English rather than Latin or Czech; the translation here preserves the content faithfully while adding bracketed technical/period terms (e.g., plantago, albumen ovi) for scholarly clarity. No illegible passages were present. The practice of delaying dryness of wounds until the third day reflects period beliefs about laudable pus and wound 'ripening' before closure.

results.title_inferred: Manuscript Description: MS XVII.J.28 (Czech National Library, Prague)
results.original_text: MS XVII.J.28, Czech National Library, Prague. 15th century medical compendium. Contains: De viribus herbarum (Macer Floridus) in Czech translation — the only surviving Czech version of this foundational medieval plant medicine text. Also contains medical recipes, practical household remedies, and the Albík advice to Emperor Sigismund. Written in Czech and Latin, likely Bohemian provenance, c. 1400–1450 CE.
results.translation: Manuscript XVII.J.28, held in the Czech National Library, Prague, is a fifteenth-century medical compendium. It contains a Czech translation of 'De viribus herbarum' (On the Powers of Herbs), attributed to Macer Floridus — the only known surviving Czech-language version of this foundational medieval work on plant medicine. The manuscript also includes medical recipes, practical household remedies, and the medical advice of Albík of Uničov (Sigismund's court physician) addressed to Emperor Sigismund. The text is composed in both Czech and Latin, and the manuscript is believed to originate from Bohemia, dating to approximately 1400–1450 CE.

entities_mentioned.name: De viribus herbarum (Macer Floridus)
entities_mentioned.notes: A widely circulated medieval Latin didactic poem on medicinal plants, traditionally attributed to 'Macer Floridus' (possibly a pseudonym; sometimes associated with Odo of Meung). This manuscript preserves the only known Czech vernacular translation.

entities_mentioned.name: Albík (Albík of Uničov)
entities_mentioned.notes: Court physician to Holy Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia Sigismund of Luxembourg; author of medical advice literature included in this compendium.
